label: the accusative -e, and marking a human object
note: Chapter 87, and it closes the CASE column at 7/7. The old note named all three pieces and the chapter takes them in that order. THE ENDING: -e marks the one a verb happens to, and unlike every case ending before it, it does not place the noun anywhere -- it says what role the noun has. The doer wears nothing. English does that job with WORD ORDER alone ('I see the teacher' against 'the teacher sees me'), so a marked object is doing work English spends its word order on. THE ANIMACY RULE, which is the part worth the chapter: the rule is not about being the object, it is about WHAT KIND OF THING the object is. A living thing acted on takes -e; a lifeless one ordinarily does not, so kuttiye takes it and pustakam does not, both sitting in the same slot before the same kind of verb. NO CLITIC: the note was right that Malayalam has none. English keeps a second form (he / him) and Spanish shrinks the object into an unstressed piece that leans on the verb; Malayalam keeps the ordinary pronoun and adds the ordinary ending, so avane costs nothing to learn. That is the generalisation the recall states and four chapters now support -- where a European language keeps a special form, Malayalam usually keeps the ordinary word and adds the ordinary ending. NO NEW VOCABULARY: adhyaapakan, kutti, pustakam, avan, kaanuka and vaayikkuka are all taught, and the joining rule (-y- after a vowel, chillu opening into a plain consonant) is the genitive's.
